children: By Vassi Chamberlain | Photography by Jesper D. Lund for WSJ. Magazine

Walking into the penthouse of the new St. Clement hotel in London, you can't miss the Thames River. The two-bedroom, two-story space is dominated by a wraparound view of the waterway and surrounding landmarks-the Houses of Parliament and Big Ben to the right, and the Tate Modern museum and Shakespeare's Globe theater to the left. The hotel, which opens this month, is the first independent hospitality venture from Soho House founder Nick Jones since he stepped down as chief executive of his private-club empire in 2022.

The opening of the first Soho House on Dean Street forever altered notions of what private clubs could be-not just stuffy places with strict vetting procedures and even stricter dress codes, but stylish hangouts where creatives and entrepreneurs could work all day and party late into the night.

With the opening of the St. Clement, Jones, 62, is poised to become a face of another reinvention: that of the hotel's neighborhood in central London, which has quietly been transforming from a lackluster tourist destination into an area of interest. "This is the original part of London," he says. "It's where the city's first luxury hotel, The Savoy, opened in 1889. Now it's all coming back here."

The St. Clement, which has 90 rooms and 15 suites in addition to the penthouse, occupies the Thames-facing part of a nine-story brutalist building erected on the Strand in the 1970s. Known as 180 the Strand, the site was acquired in 2012 by Mark Wadhwa, a longtime partner of Jones's.

Since then, media companies, fashion designers and artists have moved into the building, along with Soho House, which opened a location (and an office) there in 2021. Not long after, the publisher Condé Nast moved into a building nearby. An even newer arrival to the neighborhood is restaurateur Jeremy King, who earlier this year reopened Simpson's in the Strand, the nearly 200-year-old institution a block away from the St. Clement, which had closed in 2020.

The area now has an energy akin to that of New York's Meatpacking District in the late 1990s-or akin to that of London when Jones founded Soho House, when the city had a renegade, laid-back and puckish spirit that has been increasingly lost with the proliferation of egregiously extravagant hotels, restaurants and bars, each one somehow blander than the last.

The St. Clement, where standard rooms start at GBP800 a night (about $1,083), has an airy lobby with a midcentury modern design that features furniture by Jean Prouvé, George Nakashima and Jean Royère. "As if Claridge's and Chiltern Firehouse had a baby," Jones says of the vibe he wanted to conjure, as he led me on a tour in late June.

The hotel has no discernible reception area, just a low desk in a corner of the lobby where guests are handed a key before being shown to their accommodations. A massive figurative painting by Jones's daughter Freya Jones, a 25-year-old artist, dominates one wall, and a large Richard Prince work sits on another. The elegantly sparse interiors are the work of Alex Eagle, the London fashion and furniture designer who is married to Wadhwa, and her creative partner Sophie Hodges. Their Eagle and Hodges design firm also has an office in the 180 building.
"The look Nick created at Soho House was so iconic," Eagle says. "It got copied by everyone. He knew we had to do something new, that wasn't derivative but more eclectic."

Along with rooms and suites, there are also private apartments for sale at the St. Clement, which range in price from GBP1.2 million (about $1.6 million) to GBP30 million (about $40.6 million) and are fully serviced by the hotel. Several have already been purchased by American, British and European buyers.

After Jones shows me the lobby, we go up to the first floor, where we walk down a hall decorated with screenprints of old local maps to a guest room. "This is a bog-standard room, the worst in the building," he says jokingly as we enter. The furnishings echo the hotel's midcentury vibe. Jones points out a hidden closet for suitcases, a Hollywood-level makeup vanity and the hotel's line of custom citrus-scented bath products from the perfumer Lyn Harris.

The hotel's amenities include a spa with an 82-foot indoor pool overlooking the Thames, as well as bars and restaurants. The brasserie-like Café Clement serves an all-day menu developed by head chef Danny Bohan, formerly of the River Cafe, whose signature lobster omelet is among the fare. Bobbi's Bar, a speakeasy open till 3 a.m., has guitars and a piano for guests to play. Lunette, another restaurant, is planned to open in September under chef Florence Knight, an alumnus of London's Polpetto.

After my tour, I stop by Bobbi's. A DJ in a sharp suit is manning the turntables, and waitresses in ties and white smoking-jacket-inspired dresses-outfits of Eagle's design-scour the crowd as people dance with drinks in the air. There is no menu, you just order what you want. The place is only a few weeks old, but feels like it's been part of London's social fabric for decades.
The cabdriver who had dropped me off outside the St. Clement earlier made a comment as I paid for my fare. "It's the hot hood now."
Not many are able to read London's tea leaves better than a local cabbie. Jones is reliably among the few who can.
